The paper surveys robotic foundation models (RFMs)—large, multimodal systems that generate low‑level robot actions—and evaluates their readiness for industrial deployment, especially on collaborative robots (cobots). It frames the industrial shift from static, high‑precision automation to flexible, human‑centric cobots that require robust, adaptive, low‑latency control. RFMs are defined as embodiment‑independent models that ingest proprioception, vision and language and output actions, plans or trajectories. Sub‑categories include vision‑language‑action (VLA) models, control‑oriented models, planning‑oriented models and hybrids.  

To assess the field, the authors built three literature corpora via an automated pipeline that translates user‑provided ASQS queries into the syntaxes of arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and Semantic Scholar, merges results, removes duplicates, enriches metadata and applies a GPT‑4o relevance filter. The primary RFM corpus contains 1 025 papers (341 control or integrated RFMs, 324 manipulation‑oriented), supplemented by an industrial‑implication set (~300 papers) and a “further” set (113 papers). A review of 55 recent embodied‑AI surveys found only 11 address RFMs, all focusing on VLAs, and only two discuss industrial applications, motivating the present work’s taxonomy, deployment viewpoints and criteria‑based evaluation.

Hardware analysis shows typical cobots with 6 DOF, 5.5 kg payload, 910 mm reach and ≈0.25 kW power consumption, far lower than conventional robots (≈3 kW). Edge platforms range from NVIDIA Jetson Nano (low cost, high compute‑per‑dollar) to Jetson Thor and RTX 5090 (high throughput, >130 W), highlighting a trade‑off between compute needs of RFMs and cobot energy budgets.

From 125 industrial studies the authors extract eleven inter‑dependent requirements (adaptability, safety, multimodal HRI, fault‑aware control, precision, cost‑effective integration, explainability, data‑scarcity handling, benchmarking, governance) mapped to 47 attributes, yielding a rubric of 149 concrete criteria. An automated pipeline queries GPT‑5.1 for each paper‑criterion pair, producing binary fulfilment judgments with confidence scores. Validation on three expert‑rated papers shows 96.6 % criterion‑level accuracy, F1 = 0.762, κ = 0.744, with a conservative bias toward false negatives (22.6 % FN, 1.9 % FP).

Evaluation of 324 manipulation‑capable RFMs reveals that even the five highest‑scoring models satisfy only 11–12 % of the criteria (proportional scores 0.11–0.12). Top models are hybrids that excel on isolated implications (e.g., Gemini Robotics 1.5 scores 0.44 on adaptability/flexibility; Collab‑VLA on safety‑related criteria). Across the full corpus, breadth is highest for adaptability/flexibility (I1), benchmarking (I10) and data usage (I11) (≈0.75), but depth remains low (≈0.09). The Top‑50 subset reaches full breadth for seven implications but depth peaks at ≈0.24. Safety/compliance (I2) and real‑time performance (I6) are especially weak (depth ≈0.02–0.04). Only ≤4 % of models meet safety, interaction or real‑time criteria; ≤14 % meet robustness; benchmarking and data‑efficiency reach ≈40–45 %.

The authors conclude that RFMs have achieved notable benchmark successes but lack industrial maturity: they fall short on real‑time adaptation, dependable instruction following, safety‑critical operation and edge‑hardware compatibility. The presented taxonomy, implication framework and criteria catalogue constitute a roadmap for future work, calling for layered architectures with explicit planning, verification and safety gating, and for evaluation protocols that measure latency, failure recovery, human supervision and long‑horizon operation. Limitations include unrecoverable table reconstructions and opaque aggregation rules for total applicability scores, meaning the quantitative granularity is limited but the overall finding—that current RFMs provide shallow, fragmented solutions rather than holistic, industry‑grade autonomy—is well supported.
